arginine-aakg.summary: A pre-workout 'pump' supplement that pairs arginine with alpha-ketoglutarate to boost nitric oxide, blood flow and the full look of trained muscles.

quick.overview:
AAKG is a salt of the amino acid L-arginine and alpha-ketoglutarate, sold to lifters as a pre-workout ingredient for bigger muscle pumps, more blood flow and better training output. The payoff people are after is fuller-looking muscles in the gym and, over time, more size from harder sessions.

Arginine is the precursor of nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels, so the idea is more arginine, more nitric oxide, more blood flow into the working muscle. Published human trials are few and small, and they measured strength and endurance rather than visible muscle size; several report no change in performance from acute AAKG or arginine.
quick.how: People take it as a powder or capsule shortly before training, usually as one ingredient in a multi-ingredient pre-workout alongside caffeine and other stimulants. It is used on training days and judged by how the pump and workout feel, so results are reported within a session rather than over weeks.
quick.risks: Higher intakes can cause mild stomach upset. A 2012 case report described a hemorrhagic stroke in a young man after a multi-ingredient sports supplement containing other stimulants, so the cause cannot be pinned on AAKG alone. It is sold as a dietary supplement.

angle.text: Lifters take AAKG before training for a bigger pump and more blood flow, which they link to harder sessions and fuller-looking muscles that add up to more size over time. Small human trials have tested strength and performance rather than visible muscle size.

bcaa.summary: Leucine, isoleucine and valine powders taken around training to cut soreness and speed recovery, so you can train more and build more muscle.

quick.overview:
BCAAs are three essential amino acids found in dietary protein and sold as stand-alone powders and capsules. Lifters use them to feel less sore and recover faster, which means more frequent training and more muscle over time.

Leucine switches on the mTOR pathway that starts muscle protein synthesis, and that mechanism is well described in lab work. Human studies suggest possible reductions in muscle-damage markers and soreness, while effects on performance are described as neutral or unclear, and trials on physique outcomes from BCAA supplements specifically are limited.
quick.how: People sip BCAA drinks or take capsules before, during or after lifting, often while training fasted or on a calorie deficit. They are commonly stacked with a protein powder or creatine, and users usually notice soreness differences within days rather than visible size.
quick.risks: Sold as a dietary supplement. Higher circulating BCAAs are associated with obesity and insulin resistance, and some studies have raised questions about links with ALS in athletes and about lifespan in mice; these relationships are not fully established.

angle.text: Lifters use BCAA powders around training to cut soreness and speed recovery, so they can train more often and build a more muscular physique. Leucine's role in switching on muscle protein synthesis is well described; trials of stand-alone BCAAs for muscle gain are limited.

zma.summary: A zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6 bedtime supplement taken for deeper sleep and better recovery, which lifters link to more muscle.

quick.overview:
ZMA is a bundle of zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6, created by BALCO founder Victor Conte and sold to athletes as a pre-bed supplement. Bodybuilders take it hoping for better sleep and higher testosterone, which they tie to overnight recovery and more muscle from training.

The claimed chain is that these minerals support sleep and anabolic hormone processes, with timing before bed meant to aid absorption. A 1998 company-funded study reported strength gains in football players, while later studies, including an industry-funded one, found no significant hormone or performance effects.
quick.how: People take it as capsules on an empty stomach at night, usually as part of a general lifting and sleep routine. Users commonly judge it over several weeks by sleep quality and how recovered they feel. Some variants add 5-HTP.
quick.risks: Sold as a dietary supplement. Variants that add 5-HTP can raise serotonin, which matters if combined with serotonin-raising drugs. Published safety data are not extensively covered in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Bodybuilders take ZMA at night for better sleep and higher testosterone, which they link to recovery and muscle gain. The few studies on those outcomes in trained athletes give conflicting results.

beef-organ-beef-juice-extract.summary: Concentrated beef organ or meat-juice products used as nutrient-dense support for training, recovery and building a leaner, more muscular physique.

quick.overview:
These are products made from beef organs or concentrated beef extract, sold as capsules or food-style supplements. Users take them as a dense source of protein and micronutrients to support training, recovery and a stronger physique. Meat extract dates to Liebig in 1840, and offal is a traditional food in many cuisines.

The chain is concentrated protein and micronutrients, better recovery, then more muscle and a leaner build. The case rests mainly on general nutrition knowledge about meat and offal; no trial of a branded organ or juice supplement for muscle was found, though a small registered study looked at absorption of hydrolysed beef.
quick.how: People take organ capsules or beef-extract products daily alongside a high-protein diet, or eat liver and other offal as whole food. It is used as a background nutrition habit, so changes are judged over weeks to months of training.
quick.risks: Sold as food or supplement. Older lab studies found mutagenic compounds forming in cooked beef and beef extract; the relevance to modern products is not established. Those who need to limit certain nutrients for medical reasons should check with a clinician.

angle.text: Beef organ and beef juice products are used as nutrient-dense support so you can recover well and build a stronger, leaner physique. The case comes from general nutrition knowledge about meat and offal; product-specific trials on muscle were not found.

dimethylglycine-dmg.summary: A glycine derivative once called vitamin B16, taken for endurance and recovery so you can train more consistently.

quick.overview:
DMG is a natural metabolite of betaine and choline, found in beans and liver, and sold as a supplement for endurance, oxygen use and immune support. Users take it hoping for quicker recovery and more consistent training, which they tie to a better physique.

It sits in the methyl-donor pathway, produced from betaine and converted to sarcosine, and has acted at the NMDA receptor glycine site in mice. Trials in autism showed little difference from placebo and a Cochrane review found no benefit in mitochondrial disease; no athletic trials are cited.
quick.how: People take it as capsules or sublingual tablets, often alongside other recovery or endurance supplements, and judge it by how training and recovery feel over a few weeks.
quick.risks: In concentrated form it is labelled harmful if swallowed, and the rat oral LD50 is above 650 mg/kg. Human safety data are limited in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: DMG is sold for endurance, oxygen use and immune support, and users take it for quicker recovery and more consistent training. Trials in autism and mitochondrial disease have been small or null, and none look at appearance or training outcomes.

magnesium-glycinate.summary: A glycine-bound magnesium supplement taken for calmer sleep and recovery, which users tie to a more rested face and better training.

quick.overview:
Magnesium glycinate is magnesium bound to glycine, about 14 percent elemental magnesium, sold to correct deficiency and popular for sleep, relaxation and recovery. Looksmaxxing users take it for deeper sleep, which they link to fresher skin, less puffiness and better training.

It supplies magnesium, a mineral involved in many enzyme and nerve functions, with glycine, which proponents say adds a calming effect. Marketing describes it as gentler and better absorbed than oxide forms; trials on glycinate specifically for sleep are few, and many sleep claims rest on magnesium in general or on stacks with theanine and GABA.
quick.how: People take it as capsules or powder in the evening, usually as part of a wind-down routine and often combined with other sleep supplements. Users report changes in sleep and relaxation within days to a few weeks.
quick.risks: Diarrhoea is the main reported effect and is described as milder than with other forms. Severe renal impairment is listed as a contraindication in reference text.

angle.text: Magnesium glycinate is popular for calmer sleep, relaxation and recovery, which users tie to a more rested face and better training. Sleep claims often rest on magnesium in general or on stacks with theanine and GABA, with few glycinate-specific trials.

magnesium-malate.summary: Magnesium bound to malic acid, used for energy, less muscle soreness and faster recovery between training sessions.

quick.overview:
Magnesium malate pairs magnesium with malic acid and is sold to correct deficiency and for energy, muscle soreness and recovery. Users take it so they can train more often in pursuit of a better physique.

It supplies magnesium, which is involved in muscle and nerve function, while malate is an intermediate in energy metabolism that sellers cite for energy claims. Claims that it absorbs better than citrate or glycinate trace to a supplier source, and the European Food Safety Authority has evaluated di-magnesium malate as a food ingredient. Direct human trials on the malate form are scarce.
quick.how: People take it as capsules or tablets, often split between morning and evening, and combine it with a general recovery routine. Effects on soreness and energy are judged over a few weeks.
quick.risks: Human safety data specific to this form are limited in the sources reviewed; EFSA assessed its use in foods and supplements. As with other magnesium forms, loose stools are a common effect of higher intakes.

angle.text: Magnesium malate is used for energy, less muscle soreness and faster recovery, so users can train more often in pursuit of a better physique. Human trials on the malate form are scarce, and most claims come from supplement sellers.

inositol-nicotinate.summary: A no-flush niacin (vitamin B3) supplement taken for circulation and skin health, aiming at a healthier-looking complexion.

quick.overview:
Inositol nicotinate is niacin bound to inositol, sold as a supplement that does not cause the usual niacin flush. Users take it as a gentler route to niacin, linking vitamin B3 to circulation and a healthier complexion.

It is described as breaking down into inositol and niacin after ingestion, and limited conversion to active niacin may explain the lack of flushing. Published research concerns circulation, including Raynaud's phenomenon and leg pain on walking, with mixed results; no study examines skin or appearance.
quick.how: People take it as capsules, usually daily with food, as a flush-free alternative to regular niacin, and often alongside other skin or circulation supplements. Any change in skin is judged over weeks.
quick.risks: Generally described as safe by mouth, with stomach upset, gas, nausea and possible liver effects similar to other niacin products. Cautions are listed for diabetes, liver or kidney disease, bleeding disorders and gout. It is sold over the counter in the US.

angle.text: Inositol nicotinate is taken as a no-flush form of niacin, with users linking vitamin B3 to better circulation and a healthier complexion. It has been studied for circulation in conditions such as intermittent claudication; nothing has been published on appearance.

pyridoxamine.summary: A natural vitamin B6 form used as an AGE inhibitor to limit glycation and keep collagen and skin looking younger.

quick.overview:
Pyridoxamine is a natural form of vitamin B6 used by longevity and skin-focused people as an inhibitor of advanced glycation end products (AGEs), which are linked to tissue ageing. The appearance goal is less collagen stiffening and slower visible skin ageing.

It is reported to trap reactive carbonyl intermediates, chelate metals and scavenge radicals, limiting glycation and lipoxidation products. Its clinical development was for diabetic kidney disease and ended in 2016 when the sponsor ran out of funding; animal studies reported kidney and retina protection in diabetic rats, and no study tests it for skin.
quick.how: People take it as an oral supplement as part of a longevity or anti-ageing stack, typically with a lower-sugar diet and sun protection. Skin ageing changes are slow, so users judge it over months.
quick.risks: Safety data are not detailed in the sources reviewed. In the US the FDA ruled in 2009 that pyridoxamine products are not dietary supplements under DSHEA, so availability there is unusual.

angle.text: Longevity and skin-focused users take pyridoxamine as an AGE inhibitor, on the theory that less glycation keeps collagen supple and slows visible skin ageing. It has been studied in diabetic kidney disease and in animals; no appearance research exists.

d-ribose-l-cysteine.summary: A patented cysteine prodrug used to raise glutathione, the body's main antioxidant, for healthier and younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
D-Ribose-L-cysteine (DRLC), sold as RiboCeine and RibCys, is a branded ingredient designed to deliver cysteine for glutathione production. Users in longevity and skin circles take it to boost antioxidant protection and support a healthier, younger look.

The ribose-cysteine ring is described as resisting oxidation until a cell releases cysteine, which the body then uses to make glutathione. Published work found is in cells and animals; no human trial was found, and none addresses appearance.
quick.how: People take it as a capsule or powder as part of a longevity or antioxidant stack, often alongside or instead of N-acetylcysteine. Any skin effect would be judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found in the sources reviewed. Claims of superiority over N-acetylcysteine rest on cell-culture and animal work described by a non-peer-reviewed reference.

angle.text: DRLC is used to raise glutathione, and users in longevity and skin circles hope for antioxidant protection that supports a healthier, younger look. Research found is in cells and animals; nothing covers appearance.

eutropoflavin-7-8-dhf.summary: A plant flavone used as a BDNF mimic for mood, drive and recovery, which supports general wellbeing.

quick.overview:
7,8-DHF is a flavone reported in 2010 to mimic BDNF signalling at the TrkB receptor. Nootropic enthusiasts take it for mood, cognition and recovery; the payoff is general wellbeing and drive rather than a direct change in how you look.

It is described as binding TrkB and triggering signalling such as AKT, though a 2017 line of work questioned direct agonism. All published work found is in cells and animals, with low oral bioavailability in mice, and no human trial was found.
quick.how: People take it as capsules, often as part of a nootropic stack, and judge it by mood, focus and how recovered they feel over a few weeks. The name eutropoflavin is used in forums for 7,8-DHF, though references apply it to a related analogue.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. Some in vitro effects, such as weak aromatase inhibition, have not been confirmed in living animals. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: 7,8-DHF is used by nootropic enthusiasts as a BDNF mimic for mood, cognition and recovery, with the appearance link being general wellbeing and drive. It has been studied in cells and animals; no human studies exist.

5-htp-oxitriptan.summary: A serotonin precursor taken for mood and deeper sleep, which users link to clearer skin and a more rested face.

quick.overview:
5-HTP is the step between tryptophan and serotonin and is sold as a supplement for sleep and mood. Looksmaxxing users take it for deeper, longer sleep, which they connect to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

The body makes it from tryptophan; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to serotonin, an effect raised by decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa. Human trials are registered for depression, mood, body composition, fatigue, satiety and sleep, but the sources reviewed do not report outcomes and none targets appearance.
quick.how: People take it as capsules, usually in the evening as part of a sleep routine, and sometimes in bedtime stacks with magnesium. Effects on sleep are judged over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Serotonin syndrome is a documented concern when combined with serotonin-raising drugs such as SSRIs. No FDA-approved medicine contains 5-HTP as of 2025, and it is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: 5-HTP is taken as a serotonin precursor for mood and sleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Trials cover mood and sleep, among other conditions; none address appearance.

l-tryptophan.summary: An essential amino acid and serotonin and melatonin precursor taken for sleep and mood, which users tie to a more rested face.

quick.overview:
Tryptophan is an essential amino acid found in meat, dairy, eggs, nuts and seeds, and the starting material for serotonin, melatonin and niacin. As a supplement it is used for sleep and mood, with looksmaxxing users linking better sleep to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

Most dietary tryptophan goes down the kynurenine pathway, while a smaller share becomes serotonin and melatonin. A 2001 Cochrane review found only two eligible studies with 64 participants and judged the evidence insufficient, and a 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline advises against its use for insomnia; appearance outcomes have not been studied.
quick.how: People take it as capsules or powder in the evening, often away from protein-heavy meals and as part of a wind-down routine. Sleep effects are judged over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Side effects include nausea, drowsiness and headache; combining with SSRIs or MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome. A 1989 outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, traced largely to contaminated batches, led to US restrictions that were lifted in 2001.

angle.text: L-tryptophan is taken as a serotonin and melatonin precursor for sleep and mood, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. A 2001 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for sleep, and appearance has not been studied.

ramelteon.summary: A prescription melatonin-receptor drug for falling asleep faster, which users tie to a more rested face and clearer skin.

quick.overview:
Ramelteon (Rozerem) is a prescription drug for trouble falling asleep that works on the same receptors as the body's own melatonin rather than on the GABA system. Looksmaxxing users discuss it because better sleep is linked to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors thought to be involved in the sleep-wake rhythm and is quickly cleared from the body. Trials show it shortens the time to fall asleep by roughly 10 to 19 minutes versus placebo; no studies have examined it for appearance.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth at bedtime on prescription for sleep-onset trouble, and users judge it by how quickly they fall asleep. It is used under a doctor's care as a medical insomnia treatment.
quick.risks: Labelled adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue and nausea, with rare allergic reactions and complex sleep behaviours. It is prescription-only in the US, not a controlled substance, and not authorised in the EU.

angle.text: Ramelteon is a prescription melatonin-receptor sleep aid for trouble falling asleep, discussed on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Small medical trials cover insomnia; appearance has not been studied.

tasimelteon.summary: A prescription circadian-rhythm drug that aligns the sleep-wake cycle, used by some to chase better sleep and a more rested look.

quick.overview:
Tasimelteon (Hetlioz) is a melatonin-receptor drug approved in the US for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder, mainly seen in totally blind people, and for nighttime sleep problems in Smith-Magenis syndrome. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for aligning the sleep-wake cycle, with the hoped-for payoff of clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors involved in circadian timing, though the label says exactly how it works in Non-24 is unclear. Phase 3 trials in totally blind people reported entrainment of the circadian rhythm in a minority of patients; no research ties it to appearance.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth at a set time each night under prescription for its approved circadian conditions. It is not a general insomnia pill, and effects on the rhythm build over weeks.
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache, raised liver enzyme ALT, vivid dreams or nightmares and infections. The label warns of somnolence. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Tasimelteon is a prescription circadian-rhythm drug used to align the sleep-wake cycle, discussed on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for Non-24 disorder and Smith-Magenis sleep problems; appearance has not been studied.

agomelatine.summary: A melatonin-linked antidepressant sold in Europe, used for better sleep and lower stress that users tie to a fresher face.

quick.overview:
Agomelatine (Valdoxan) is a prescription antidepressant authorised in the EU since 2009 and in some other countries, but not in the US. Users consider it for its sleep and mood effects, with the hoped-for payoff of lower stress and a fresher, more rested face.

It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors and blocks 5-HT2C receptors, which preclinical work links to increased dopamine and noradrenaline in the frontal cortex. Network meta-analyses have compared it with other antidepressants for major depression; no study has examined appearance.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth in the evening on prescription for depression, with liver testing as part of use. Mood and sleep effects are judged over weeks.
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache, nausea, dizziness and sleepiness. Raised liver enzymes have been reported, so liver testing is part of use, and it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment. It is not FDA approved.

angle.text: Agomelatine is a melatonin-linked antidepressant that some users consider for sleep and mood, on the theory that better sleep and lower stress show up in the face. It is studied for depression; appearance has not been studied.

hydroxyzine.summary: A sedating prescription antihistamine for anxiety, itch and sleep, used to get more rested nights and calmer skin.

quick.overview:
Hydroxyzine is an older prescription antihistamine, approved by the FDA in 1956, used for anxiety and tension, allergic itching and sedation around surgery. Looksmaxxing users discuss it for its sedating and anti-itch effects, tying better sleep to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

It blocks histamine H1 receptors and, because it enters the brain, causes sedation. It is studied for anxiety disorders and urticaria; no studies look at its effect on appearance.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth on prescription, often in the evening because of the drowsiness, for anxiety or itch. Sedation is felt within the first hours after a dose.
quick.risks: Drowsiness, dry mouth and dizziness are common. Labels warn about combined sedation with alcohol and other depressants, rare heart rhythm effects and seizures, and use in early pregnancy.

angle.text: Hydroxyzine is a sedating antihistamine used for anxiety, itch and sleep, discussed on the theory that better sleep and calmer skin show up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for anxiety and itch; its effect on looks has not been studied.

low-dose-doxepin-silenor.summary: A prescription low-dose tricyclic approved for staying asleep through the night, used for more rested, fresher-looking mornings.

quick.overview:
Low-dose doxepin (Silenor) is a prescription sleep medicine approved in 2010 for insomnia with difficulty staying asleep. It is a tricyclic antidepressant sold at much lower strengths for this purpose. Looksmaxxing users discuss it for sleeping through the night, linking it to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

At low strengths it mainly blocks histamine H1 receptors, producing sedation; at antidepressant strengths reuptake inhibition predominates. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2017 guideline includes low-dose doxepin among its recommendations for sleep-maintenance insomnia; no studies examine appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as a tablet shortly before bed on prescription for sleep-maintenance insomnia. Effects on staying asleep show up from the first nights.
quick.risks: Reported effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation and blood pressure drops on standing. It is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors and is prescription-only.

angle.text: Low-dose doxepin is a prescription option for staying asleep through the night, discussed on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for sleep-maintenance insomnia; appearance has not been studied.

suvorexant.summary: A prescription orexin-blocking sleep drug that helps you fall and stay asleep, used for a more rested, fresher-looking face.

quick.overview:
Suvorexant (Belsomra) is a prescription insomnia drug approved in 2014 that blocks the brain's wake-promoting orexin signals. Looksmaxxing users discuss it because better sleep is linked to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

It competitively blocks orexin A and B at OX1 and OX2 receptors, reducing arousal rather than broadly depressing the central nervous system through GABA. Randomised trials, including a one-year trial, reported improvements in time to fall asleep and time awake; no studies look at appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as a tablet at bedtime on prescription for trouble falling or staying asleep. Sleep effects are noticed from the first nights.
quick.risks: Next-day somnolence, headache and dizziness are reported, with rare complex sleep behaviours. It is Schedule IV in the US and interacts with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and alcohol.

angle.text: Suvorexant is an orexin-blocking prescription sleep drug, discussed on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Trials show improved sleep latency and wake time in insomnia; appearance has not been studied.

lemborexant.summary: A prescription orexin-blocking sleep drug (Dayvigo) for falling and staying asleep, used for a more rested, fresher-looking face.

quick.overview:
Lemborexant (Dayvigo) is a prescription insomnia medicine from the orexin-antagonist class, approved for adults who have trouble falling or staying asleep. Looksmaxxing users discuss it through the idea that better sleep supports recovery, clearer skin and a more rested face.

It blocks orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R, reducing the wake-promoting signal in the brain, rather than boosting GABA like benzodiazepines and Z-drugs. Phase 3 trials have compared it with placebo and with zolpidem extended-release in older adults, and a 12-month trial reported longer-term data; none look at appearance.
quick.how: It is taken as a tablet at bedtime on prescription for insomnia. Users judge it by how quickly they fall asleep and how well they stay asleep.
quick.risks: Reported effects include sleepiness, headache and abnormal dreams; the label also warns of next-day impairment, sleep paralysis, complex sleep behaviors and worsening depression. It is prescription-only and Schedule IV in the US.

angle.text: Lemborexant is an orexin-blocking prescription sleep drug (Dayvigo), discussed on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It has been studied for insomnia; no appearance studies exist.
